sentences.text: This petition under Section 482 of Cr.P.C. has been filed seeking quashment of RCT No.1230of 2021 pending in the Court of JMFC, Jabalpur arising out of FIR No.445 of 2020 for the offences punishable under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code, Section 3 & 7 of the Essential Commodities Act, Section 7 of Urvarak (Niyantran) Aadesh, 1985 and Section 14(a), 14(b), 10(4), 29(3) and 33 of the Keetnashak Adhiniayam registered at Police Station Madhotal, Jabalpur against the petitioner.

2. The prosecution case, in nutshell, is that a written complaint has been made by the respondent No.2 with regard to illegal manufacturing of spurious fertilizers, pesticides and fungicides, mixing of Mahesh Khatri vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 18 August, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/139626303/

sentences.text: After investigation, the applicant has been charged sheeted for the aforesaid offences.

3. Learned counsel for the applicant has contended that allegation against the present applicant is that he being the real younger brother of main accused Mayank Khatri is liable for all the offences.
The applicant is having virtually no connection with the crime in question.
Therefore, registration of the FIR against the present applicant is per se illegal.
He has prayed for quashment of FIR and all subsequent proceedings incidental to it.

4. Per contra, learned counsel for the State has vehemently opposed the contentions stating that there are sufficient material available in the charge sheet so as to suggest that the applicant is prima facie involved in the offences with which he is charged with.
Hence, no interference is required in the matter.

5. Heard the counsel for the parties and perused the record.
6.

The law with respect to quashment of FIR has been considered by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in large number of cases as in the cases of Umendra @ Banti Vs. State of M.P. reported in 2016 (1)
MPLJ (Cri) 93, Mosiruddin Munshi Vs. Md. Siraj & Anr. reported in 2014 CRLR (SC) 548, Tilly Gifford Vs. Michael Floyd Eshwar reported in 2018 (11) SCC 205, Munshiram Vs. State of Rajasthan and another reported in 2018 (5) SCC 678, State of Tamil Nadu Vs. S. Martin and others reported in 2018 (5) SCC 718, Dineshbhai Chandubhai Patel Vs. State of Gujarat and others reported in 2018 (2)
JLJ 373 and recently in the case of Niharika Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. vs. State of Maharashtra and Others reported in 2021 SCC Online 315 by considering the landmark judgment of State of Haryana Vs. Bhajanlal reported in 1992 Suppl. SCC 335 has framed certain guidelines for consideration of cases for quashment of FIR especially in paragraph 80, which read as under :-
"80.

sentences.text: Therefore, when the investigation by the police is in progress, the court should not go into the merits of the allegations in the FIR.
Police must be permitted to complete the investigation.
It would b e premature to pronounce the conclusion based on hazy facts that the complaint/FIR does not deserve to be investigated or that it amounts to abuse of process of law.

After investigation, if the investigating officer finds that there is no substance in the application made by the complainant, the investigating officer may file an appropriate report/summary before the learned Magistrate which may be considered by the learned Magistrate in accordance with the known procedure;
xiii) The power under Section 482 Cr.P.C. is very wide, but conferment of wide power requires the court to be more cautious.

sentences.text: However, at the same time, the court, if it thinks fit, regard being had to the parameters of quashing and the self-restraint imposed by law, more particularly the parameters laid down by this Court in the cases of R.P. Kapur (supra) and Bhajan Lal (supra), has the jurisdiction to quash the FIR/complaint;

xv) When a prayer for quashing the FIR is made by the alleged accused and the court when it exercises the power under Section 482 Cr.P.C., only has to consider whether the allegations in the FIR disclose commission of a cognizable offence or not.

The court is not required to consider on merits whether or not the merits of the allegations make out a cognizable offence and the court has to permit the investigating agency/police to investigate the allegations in the FIR;

xvi) The aforesaid parameters would be applicable and/or the aforesaid aspects are required to be considered by the High Court while passing an interim order in a quashing petition in exercise of powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C. and/or under Article 226 of the Constitution of India.

However,
an interim order of stay of investigation during the pendency of the quashing petition can be passed with circumspection.
Such an interim order should not require to be passed routinely, casually and/or mechanically.

Normally, when the investigation is in progress and the facts are hazy and the entire evidence/material is not before the High Court, the High Court should restrain itself from passing the interim order of not to arrest or ''no coercive steps to be adopted and the accused should be relegated to apply for anticipatory bail under Section 438 Cr.P.C. before the competent court.
The involvement of the applicant is clearly reflected in the case and his name appears in the FIR as well as in the statement of the witnesses.
At this stage, this Court cannot go into the minute details of the complaint and evidence available on record.
Prima facie case is required to be seen at the time of registration of FIR.
It is settled principles of law that FIR is not an encyclopedia and cannot contain all the details particulars of the crime.
These are the matter of trial to be considered by leading appropriate evidence before the learned trial Court.
Under these circumstances, no case for quashment of FIR and the subsequent criminal proceedings is made out.

Such an interim order should not require to be passed routinely, casually and/or mechanically.

The High Court shall not and as such is not justified in passing the order of not to arrest and/or ''no coercive steps either during the investigation or till the investigation is completed and/or till the final report/chargesheet is filed under Section 173 Cr.P.C., while dismissing/disposing of the quashing petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C. and/or under Article 226 of the Constitution of India;
xvii) Even in a case where the High Court is prima facie of the opinion that an exceptional case is made out for grant of interim stay of further investigation, after considering the broad parameters while exercising the powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C. and/or under Article 226 of the Constitution of India referred to hereinabove, the High Court has to give brief reasons why such an interim order is warranted and/or is required to be passed so that it can demonstrate the application of mind by the Court and the higher forum can consider what was weighed with the High Court while passing such an interim order; xviii) Whenever an interim order is passed by the High Court of no coercive steps to be adopted within the aforesaid parameters, the High Court must clarify what does it mean by ''no coercive steps to be adopted as the term ''no coercive steps to be adopted can be said to be too vague and/or broad which can be misunderstood and/or misapplied."
